techniques.name: Platt Scaling
techniques.description: Platt scaling turns a classifier's raw scores into calibrated probabilities, meaning that among the cases given a probability of 0.3, about 30 per cent turn out to be positive. It was introduced for support vector machines, whose outputs are distances from a decision boundary rather than probabilities, and applies to any binary classifier that produces a real-valued score. After the classifier is trained, a two-parameter logistic (sigmoid) curve, P(y = 1 | f) = 1 / (1 + exp(A·f + B)), is fitted by maximum likelihood to map each score f to a probability, using labelled cases the classifier was not trained on, taken from a held-out set or from cross-validation folds. The fitted curve is strictly monotonic, so the order of cases and ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve (how well the scores separate the two classes) are unchanged; only the probability attached to each case moves. The output is a recalibrated model, assessed before and after with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and with the Brier score or log loss (two measures of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened).

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's credit-risk team finds that its gradient-boosted default model ranks applicants well but squeezes predicted default probabilities towards the middle of the range. Before the probabilities feed expected-loss provisioning, the team fits Platt scaling on a held-out year of loan outcomes and checks on a reliability diagram that predicted and observed default rates agree in every score decile.

A benefits agency uses a linear support vector machine to flag claims for manual review, but its margin scores mean nothing to caseworkers. The team applies Platt scaling so the review screen can show the probability that a claim needs correcting, publishes the calibration curve in the caseworker guidance, and explains that the figure is a rate across similar claims rather than a verdict on the individual.

limitations.description: The sigmoid shape is an assumption. It corrects the S-shaped distortion typical of support vector machines and boosted trees, whose probabilities bunch towards the middle, but not the reverse distortion of overconfident models such as naive Bayes, whose probabilities pile up near 0 and 1. Where the reliability diagram shows that pattern, a flexible method such as isotonic regression is needed.

It works best when the classifier's scores for the two classes are spread in a similar way (roughly normal with equal variance). In highly imbalanced problems the scores of the two classes do not have equal spread, so the sigmoid can be a poor match for the data.

The curve should be fitted on labelled cases that played no part in training. The classifier separates its own training data better than new data, so a curve fitted to training scores overstates confidence in use; the cost is a held-out calibration set taken from scarce labelled data, or cross-validation with several model fits.

A single curve fitted across the whole population does not make the model calibrated within each subgroup. In a deployed malnutrition-risk model, recalibration improved calibration within each race and sex group, yet intercepts and slopes still differed significantly between Black and White patients. Fitting a curve per group needs group membership at prediction time, which may be unavailable or unlawful to use, and enough labelled cases in every group.

Recalibration changes every probability, so a decision threshold chosen on the raw scores no longer flags the same cases. After logistic recalibration of a deployed malnutrition-risk model, specificity rose from 0.74 to 0.93 and sensitivity fell from 0.75 to 0.35, so the cut-off has to be reset against the cost of each kind of error and the downstream process checked again.

resources.title: Assessing calibration and bias of a deployed machine learning malnutrition prediction model within a large healthcare system
resources.abstract: Malnutrition is a frequently underdiagnosed condition leading to increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. The Mount Sinai Health System (MSHS) deployed a machine learning model (MUST-Plus) to detect malnutrition upon hospital admission. However, in diverse patient groups, a poorly calibrated model may lead to misdiagnosis, exacerbating health care disparities. We explored the model’s calibration across different variables and methods to improve calibration. Data from adult patients admitted to five MSHS hospitals from January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, were analyzed. We compared MUST-Plus prediction to the registered dietitian’s formal assessment. Hierarchical calibration was assessed and compared between the recalibration sample (N = 49,562) of patients admitted between January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, and the hold-out sample (N = 17,278) of patients admitted between January 1, 2023 - September 30, 2023. Statistical differences in calibration metrics were tested using bootstrapping with replacement. Before recalibration, the overall model calibration intercept was −1.17 (95% CI: −1.20, −1.14), slope was 1.37 (95% CI: 1.34, 1.40), and Brier score was 0.26 (95% CI: 0.25, 0.26). Both weak and moderate measures of calibration were significantly different between White and Black patients and between male and female patients. Logistic recalibration significantly improved calibration of the model across race and gender in the hold-out sample. The original MUST-Plus model showed significant differences in calibration between White vs. Black patients. It also overestimated malnutrition in females compared to males. Logistic recalibration effectively reduced miscalibration across all patient subgroups. Continual monitoring and timely recalibration can improve model accuracy.

sample_claims.text: After Platt scaling on a held-out year of loan outcomes, the default model's predicted probabilities agree with observed default rates in every score decile, within the tolerance set in the model risk policy.

After Platt scaling, the defect classifier's log loss on the held-out test set is lower than before, and its reliability diagram shows predicted defect rates within the tolerance set in the quality plan.

Each flagged claim is shown to caseworkers with a probability calibrated against held-out review outcomes, and the calibration curve and its meaning are published in the caseworker guidance, so a displayed 30 per cent corresponds to roughly 30 in 100 similar claims needing correction.

techniques.name: Machine Unlearning
techniques.description: Machine unlearning enables removal of specific training data's influence from trained models without complete retraining. This technique addresses privacy rights like GDPR's right to be forgotten by selectively erasing learned patterns associated with particular data points, individuals, or sensitive attributes. Methods include exact unlearning (provably equivalent to retraining without the data), approximate unlearning (efficient algorithms that closely approximate retraining), and certified unlearning (providing formal guarantees about information removal).

example_use_cases.description: Responding to user deletion requests in a social media recommendation system by removing all influence of that user's historical interactions, ensuring GDPR compliance and verifiable data removal.

Enabling a financial institution to demonstrate regulatory compliance by providing cryptographic proof that a former customer's transaction history has been completely removed from credit risk assessment models following account closure.

limitations.description: Exact unlearning for complex models like deep neural networks is computationally expensive, often nearly as costly as full retraining.
Approximate unlearning methods may not provide strong guarantees that information has been fully removed, potentially leaving residual influence.
Difficult to verify unlearning effectiveness, as adversaries might extract information about supposedly removed data through membership inference or other attacks.
Repeated unlearning requests can degrade model performance significantly, especially if many data points are removed from the training distribution.
Requires access to model architecture and training process details (white-box access), making it difficult to apply to third-party models or models where internal structure is proprietary.
Particularly challenging for very large foundation models where even storing checkpoints for potential retraining is infeasible, limiting practical applicability to smaller, domain-specific models.

resources.title: Digital forgetting in large language models: A survey of unlearning methods
resources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become the state of the art in natural language processing. The massive adoption of generative LLMs and the capabilities they have shown have prompted public concerns regarding their impact on the labor market, privacy, the use of copyrighted work, and how these models align with human ethics and the rule of law. As a response, new regulations are being pushed, which require developers and service providers to evaluate, monitor, and forestall or at least mitigate the risks posed by their models. One mitigation strategy is digital forgetting: given a model with undesirable knowledge or behavior, the goal is to obtain a new model where the detected issues are no longer present. Digital forgetting is usually enforced via machine unlearning techniques, which modify trained machine learning models for them to behave as models trained on a subset of the original training data. In this work, we describe the motivations and desirable properties of digital forgetting when applied to LLMs, and we survey recent works on machine unlearning. Specifically, we propose a taxonomy of unlearning methods based on the reach and depth of the modifications done on the models, we discuss and compare the effectiveness of machine unlearning methods for LLMs proposed so far, and we survey their evaluation. Finally, we describe open problems of machine unlearning applied to LLMs and we put forward recommendations for developers and practitioners.

resources.title: Towards Making Systems Forget with Machine Unlearning
resources.abstract: Today's systems produce a rapidly exploding amount of data, and the data further derives more data, forming a complex data propagation network that we call the data's lineage. There are many reasons that users want systems to forget certain data including its lineage. From a privacy perspective, users who become concerned with new privacy risks of a system often want the system to forget their data and lineage. From a security perspective, if an attacker pollutes an anomaly detector by injecting manually crafted data into the training data set, the detector must forget the injected data to regain security. From a usability perspective, a user can remove noise and incorrect entries so that a recommendation engine gives useful recommendations. Therefore, we envision forgetting systems, capable of forgetting certain data and their lineages, completely and quickly. This paper focuses on making learning systems forget, the process of which we call machine unlearning, or simply unlearning. We present a general, efficient unlearning approach by transforming learning algorithms used by a system into a summation form. To forget a training data sample, our approach simply updates a small number of summations -- asymptotically faster than retraining from scratch. Our approach is general, because the summation form is from the statistical query learning in which many machine learning algorithms can be implemented. Our approach also applies to all stages of machine learning, including feature selection and modeling. Our evaluation, on four diverse learning systems and real-world workloads, shows that our approach is general, effective, fast, and easy to use.

resources.title: Machine Unlearning
resources.abstract: Once users have shared their data online, it is generally difficult for them to revoke access and ask for the data to be deleted. Machine learning (ML) exacerbates this problem because any model trained with said data may have memorized it, putting users at risk of a successful privacy attack exposing their information. Yet, having models unlearn is notoriously difficult.We introduce SISA training, a framework that expedites the unlearning process by strategically limiting the influence of a data point in the training procedure. While our framework is applicable to any learning algorithm, it is designed to achieve the largest improvements for stateful algorithms like stochastic gradient descent for deep neural networks. SISA training reduces the computational overhead associated with unlearning, even in the worst-case setting where unlearning requests are made uniformly across the training set. In some cases, the service provider may have a prior on the distribution of unlearning requests that will be issued by users. We may take this prior into account to partition and order data accordingly, and further decrease overhead from unlearning.Our evaluation spans several datasets from different domains, with corresponding motivations for unlearning. Under no distributional assumptions, for simple learning tasks, we observe that SISA training improves time to unlearn points from the Purchase dataset by 4.63×, and 2.45× for the SVHN dataset, over retraining from scratch. SISA training also provides a speed-up of 1.36× in retraining for complex learning tasks such as ImageNet classification; aided by transfer learning, this results in a small degradation in accuracy. Our work contributes to practical data governance in machine unlearning.

resources.title: Recommendation Unlearning
resources.abstract: Recommender systems provide essential web services by learning users’ personal preferences from collected data. However, in many cases, systems also need to forget some training data. From the perspective of privacy, users desire a tool to erase the impacts of their sensitive data from the trained models. From the perspective of utility, if a system’s utility is damaged by some bad data, the system needs to forget such data to regain utility. While unlearning is very important, it has not been well-considered in existing recommender systems. Although there are some researches have studied the problem of machine unlearning, existing methods can not be directly applied to recommendation as they are unable to consider the collaborative information.

sample_claims.text: The model demonstrably excludes the influence of withdrawn patient records without requiring complete retraining of the clinical risk assessment system
The recommendation system provides verifiable evidence that deleted user data no longer affects personalized content rankings following account closure requests
The system documents which training examples have been removed and provides formal guarantees about the completeness of their erasure from model behavior

techniques.name: Isotonic Regression Calibration
techniques.description: Isotonic regression calibration turns a classifier's scores into calibrated probabilities by fitting a step-shaped function that never decreases as the score rises. Unlike a fixed curve, it assumes nothing about the shape of the miscalibration except that a higher score should never mean a lower chance of the positive outcome, so it can correct any distortion that leaves the cases in the right order. It is fitted on labelled cases the classifier was not trained on: the cases are sorted by score, and the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm repeatedly merges neighbouring groups whose observed positive rates are out of order, until the rates rise steadily with the score. Each merged group's observed rate becomes the calibrated probability for scores in its range, and the result is assessed with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and the Brier score (a measure of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened) before and after.

example_use_cases.description: A clinical research team builds a random forest on electronic health records to predict which adolescents will attempt suicide. The forest ranks patients well, but its vote shares are not probabilities, so the team fits isotonic regression on held-out records and reports calibration slope, intercept and Brier score before the risk estimates are used to prioritise clinical follow-up.

An insurer's pricing team applies isotonic recalibration to the output of its claim-probability model, fitted on a large portfolio and checked on a later year of policies, so that within each band of predicted risk the average prediction matches the observed claim rate and no price band systematically subsidises another.

An online marketplace scores listings for fraud with a naive Bayes text classifier whose probabilities cluster near 0 and 1, and analysts had been treating them as near-certainties. With tens of thousands of labelled past cases available, the team fits isotonic calibration so the review queue shows probabilities that match observed fraud rates, and shares the reliability diagram with the analysts.

limitations.description: It needs plenty of calibration data. With fewer than about a thousand labelled cases the step function follows noise in the calibration set. Because each step matches the observed rate exactly on the cases it was fitted to, calibration checked on those same cases looks perfect whatever its true quality, so it must be checked on separate cases. The two-parameter curve of Platt scaling usually does as well or better on small sets; isotonic regression pays off when calibration data are plentiful.

The output is a step function, so many different scores receive exactly the same probability. These ties discard distinctions the model made within a step, can change ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve after calibration, and matter when a decision threshold falls inside a wide step.

It relies on the classifier's ordering being right: a higher score must never mean a lower chance of the outcome. Where the model ranks cases wrongly over some range of scores, isotonic regression cannot repair the ranking and instead flattens that range into a single probability.

Probabilities at the extremes rest on little data. The outermost steps can be fitted from a handful of cases and may sit at or near 0 or 1, and common implementations clip scores beyond the range seen in calibration to the end values, so the most extreme predictions are the least trustworthy.

resources.title: Transforming classifier scores into accurate multiclass probability estimates
resources.abstract: Class membership probability estimates are important for many applications of data mining in which classification outputs are combined with other sources of information for decision-making, such as example-dependent misclassification costs, the outputs of other classifiers, or domain knowledge. Previous calibration methods apply only to two-class problems. Here, we show how to obtain accurate probability estimates for multiclass problems by combining calibrated binary probability estimates. We also propose a new method for obtaining calibrated two-class probability estimates that can be applied to any classifier that produces a ranking of examples. Using naive Bayes and support vector machine classifiers, we give experimental results from a variety of two-class and multiclass domains, including direct marketing, text categorization and digit recognition.

resources.title: Predicting suicide attempts in adolescents with longitudinal clinical data and machine learning
resources.abstract: Background Adolescents have high rates of nonfatal suicide attempts, but clinically practical risk prediction remains a challenge. Screening can be time consuming to implement at scale, if it is done at all. Computational algorithms may predict suicide risk using only routinely collected clinical data. We used a machine learning approach validated on longitudinal clinical data in adults to address this challenge in adolescents. Methods This is a retrospective, longitudinal cohort study. Data were collected from the Vanderbilt Synthetic Derivative from January 1998 to December 2015 and included 974 adolescents with nonfatal suicide attempts and multiple control comparisons: 496 adolescents with other self‐injury ( OSI ), 7,059 adolescents with depressive symptoms, and 25,081 adolescent general hospital controls. Candidate predictors included diagnostic, demographic, medication, and socioeconomic factors. Outcome was determined by multiexpert review of electronic health records. Random forests were validated with optimism adjustment at multiple time points (from 1 week to 2 years). Recalibration was done via isotonic regression. Evaluation metrics included discrimination ( AUC , sensitivity/specificity, precision/recall) and calibration (calibration plots, slope/intercept, Brier score). Results Computational models performed well and did not require face‐to‐face screening. Performance improved as suicide attempts became more imminent. Discrimination was good in comparison with OSI controls ( AUC = 0.83 [0.82–0.84] at 720 days; AUC = 0.85 [0.84–0.87] at 7 days) and depressed controls ( AUC = 0.87 [95% CI 0.85–0.90] at 720 days; 0.90 [0.85–0.94] at 7 days) and best in comparison with general hospital controls ( AUC 0.94 [0.92–0.96] at 720 days; 0.97 [0.95–0.98] at 7 days). Random forests significantly outperformed logistic regression in every comparison. Recalibration improved performance as much as ninefold – clinical recommendations with poorly calibrated predictions can lead to decision errors. Conclusions Machine learning on longitudinal clinical data may provide a scalable approach to broaden screening for risk of nonfatal suicide attempts in adolescents.

sample_claims.text: The recalibrated suicide-attempt risk model's predicted probabilities match observed attempt rates across risk deciles in held-out records, with calibration slope and intercept within pre-agreed bounds.

Within each band of predicted claim probability, the average prediction on a later, held-out year of policies is within the tolerance in the pricing policy of the observed claim rate, so no band of policyholders systematically subsidises another.

The fraud probabilities shown to analysts were recalibrated on more than 10,000 labelled past cases and agree with observed fraud rates on held-out cases, and the reliability diagram is published alongside the review tool.

techniques.name: Model Signing
techniques.description: Model signing lets the publisher of a machine-learning model attach a cryptographic signature to the model's files, so that anyone who later loads them can check who released them and that no file has changed since. Under the Open Source Security Foundation's Model Signing (OMS) specification and its reference tool, model-signing, the publisher computes a hash (a short fingerprint that changes if a single byte of the file changes) of every file in the model directory, such as weights, configuration, tokeniser and any dataset files kept with them, lists the hashes in a sorted manifest and signs the manifest, producing a detached signature file kept beside the model. The signature can be made with the publisher's own key, with a certificate from an organisation's certificate authority, or through Sigstore, which issues a short-lived certificate tied to a verified online identity, such as a person's account or a build pipeline's, and records each signing event in a transparency log, an append-only record that can be inspected afterwards. Before loading, the consumer verifies the signature against the signer it expects, recomputes every hash and rejects the model if any listed file differs or is missing or, unless that check is switched off, an unlisted file has appeared, so the evidence is a pass or fail tied to a named signer and an exact set of files. Unlike the unsigned file hashes kept by data-versioning tools, it shows who stands behind the files, and unlike a watermark, which is trained into the weights so that it survives in an altered copy, it is broken by any change; it says nothing about how the model behaves or what it was trained on.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's machine-learning platform team signs each model at the end of its training pipeline, using the pipeline's own workload identity through Sigstore, and configures its model-serving cluster to load only models whose signature verifies against that identity. Its security team watches the transparency log for signing events under that identity that match no approved release, to decide whether a model reached production outside the release process.

A vehicle maker's perception team downloads a pretrained object detector from a supplier catalogue that signs every model it publishes. Before fine-tuning, it verifies the download against the supplier's published certificate and files the verification output in its supplier-acceptance record, so later reviews can show exactly which files the work started from.

A hospital's imaging department receives quarterly updates to a vendor's chest X-ray triage model. Its clinical engineering team verifies each update against the vendor's certificate and rejects any update whose signature fails, or that contains a file the signature does not cover, before it enters the clinical validation environment.

A public research institute releases an open model together with the test set behind its published benchmark, signing both in one bundle, so that a laboratory re-running the benchmark can confirm that the weights and the test data are byte for byte the ones the institute released before comparing its results with the published ones.

limitations.description: It shows who released the files and that they have not changed, nothing more. A model carrying a malicious pickle payload, a backdoor or the effects of poisoned training data verifies perfectly if its publisher signed it, whether through carelessness or because the publisher's own pipeline was compromised before signing. The originating paper states that signing tells the user nothing about what a model does or how it was produced, so content checks are still needed.

A valid signature is only as good as the consumer's check of who made it. A model signed with an attacker's own identity, or by an account named to look like a well-known organisation (a documented attack on model hubs), verifies cleanly unless the verifier insists on the specific identity, certificate or public key it expects. Consumers need a maintained list of trusted signers for each model source.

A stolen signing key, or a compromised account at the identity provider used for Sigstore signing, produces valid signatures. With Sigstore every signature is recorded in a transparency log, so a publisher that monitors the log for its own identity can spot signatures it did not make; with the key and certificate methods the specification does not require a log entry, so misuse of a key may go unnoticed.

Any change to the files breaks verification, including legitimate ones such as quantisation, conversion to another file format or adding a file. Each derived model needs a new signature from whoever produced it, and that signature says nothing about how the derivative relates to the signed original; recording that relationship needs a separate provenance record, such as the pedigree section of an ML-BOM.

It protects only where verification is enforced. Most models on public hubs are unsigned (fewer than 2% of Hugging Face models used the hub's GPG commit-signing option, per studies the originating paper cites), and an unchecked signature protects nobody. Verification re-hashes every file, and hashing dominates the cost: a 1 TB file took about 13 minutes on a 128-vCPU server in the originating paper's benchmark, which matters if very large models are verified at every load.

resources.title: Position: Machine Learning Models Have a Supply Chain Problem
resources.abstract: Powerful machine learning (ML) models are now readily available online, which creates exciting possibilities for users who lack the deep technical expertise or substantial computing resources needed to develop them. On the other hand, this type of open ecosystem comes with many risks. In this paper, we argue that the current ecosystem for open ML models contains significant supply-chain risks, some of which have been exploited already in real attacks. These include an attacker replacing a model with something malicious (e.g., malware), or a model being trained using a vulnerable version of a framework or on restricted or poisoned data. We then explore how Sigstore, a solution designed to bring transparency to open-source software supply chains, can be used to bring transparency to open ML models, in terms of enabling model publishers to sign their models and prove properties about the datasets they use.
